name: Hand and wrist bones (right)
description: Right hand and wrist skeleton: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges, with the distal radius and ulna for context.

source.attribution: BodyParts3D, (c) The Database Center for Life Science, licensed under CC Attribution-Share Alike 2.1 Japan
source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred on the hand, one node per structure. Geometry otherwise unchanged.
source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken unchanged from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved).

groups.label: Carpal bones
groups.tip: So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb. The top row runs scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, then the bottom row comes back: hamate, capitate, trapezoid, trapezium.

groups.label: Metacarpals
groups.tip: The metacarpals are numbered one to five, starting at the thumb. Make a fist, and their heads are your knuckles.

groups.label: Phalanges
groups.tip: Each finger has three phalanges, but the thumb has only two. That makes 14 in each hand.

content.origin: From the Latin word for the spoke of a wheel. It swings around the ulna like a spoke turning on a wheel.
content.location: It is the forearm bone on your thumb side. Its wide lower end makes up most of your wrist joint.
content.description: A long bone that starts slim at the elbow and flares out wide at the wrist, a bit like a trumpet.
content.function: It takes most of the load from your hand. It also rolls around the ulna so you can turn your palm up and down.
content.mnemonic: Give a thumbs up. The radius runs down to your thumb, so it is thumbs up for the radius.
content.clinical: Fall on an outstretched hand and this bone often snaps just above the wrist. This common break is called a Colles fracture.
content.hint: Look for the big forearm bone on the thumb side, meeting the boat-shaped and moon-shaped wrist bones.

questions.text: Which movement needs the radius to roll around the ulna?
options: Turning the palm up and down
questions.explanation: When you turn a key or a door handle, your radius rolls around the ulna to turn your palm up and down.

content.origin: From the Latin word for elbow or forearm. Fitting, because its top end forms the point of your elbow.
content.location: It is the forearm bone on your little-finger side. Run a finger from your elbow point towards your little finger and you trace it.
content.description: A long bone that is chunky at the elbow and slim at the wrist, the opposite of the radius. It ends in a small point called the styloid process.
content.function: It forms the main hinge of your elbow and stays still while the radius turns around it. At the wrist, a pad of cartilage sits between it and the wrist bones.
content.mnemonic: Remember the pair: thumbs up for the radius, pinky out for the ulna.
content.clinical: When the wrist end of the radius breaks, the tiny pointed tip of the ulna often snaps off too.
content.hint: Look for the forearm bone on the little-finger side of the wrist.

questions.text: At the wrist, what sits between the ulna and the wrist bones?
options: Nothing, it touches the lunate directly
questions.explanation: A small disc of cartilage cushions the gap between the ulna and the wrist bones. It is part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex.

content.origin: From the Greek word for boat. Its long, curved shape looks a little like a small boat.
content.location: It sits in the first row of wrist bones on the thumb side, right next to the radius.
content.description: The biggest bone in the first row of the wrist. It is long and curved and reaches across towards the second row, like a bridge.
content.function: It links the two rows of wrist bones, keeping your wrist smooth and steady. It also passes force from the thumb side of your hand to the radius.
content.mnemonic: Picture a little boat sailing beside your thumb. That boat is the scaphoid.
content.clinical: It is the wrist bone people break most, usually in a fall on an outstretched hand. Pain in the hollow at the base of the thumb is a warning sign, as this bone can lose its blood supply.
content.hint: Start at the radius and step into the first row of wrist bones on the thumb side.

questions.text: Which wrist bone do people break most often?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the most often broken wrist bone. It usually happens in a fall onto an outstretched hand.

questions.text: What is an important job of the scaphoid?
options: It links the two rows of wrist bones
It forms the index finger knuckle
questions.explanation: The scaphoid bridges the two rows of wrist bones, which keeps the wrist moving smoothly and steadily.

content.origin: From the Latin word for moon. Seen from the side, it has a crescent-moon shape.
content.location: It sits in the middle of the first row of wrist bones, between the scaphoid and the triquetrum.
content.description: A small crescent-shaped bone right in the middle of your wrist, directly in line with the radius.
content.function: It helps form the main wrist joint with the radius. It passes force from the capitate, the big central wrist bone, up into your forearm.
content.mnemonic: Lunate sounds like lunar. Picture a moon rising in the middle of your wrist.
content.clinical: It is the wrist bone that most often slips out of place, or dislocates. If it loses its blood supply, it can slowly collapse, a condition called Kienbock disease.
content.hint: Look for the bone in the very middle of the first row of wrist bones.

questions.text: Which wrist bone most often slips out of place?
questions.explanation: The lunate is the wrist bone most often dislocated, meaning it is pushed out of its normal spot.

questions.text: Where is the lunate?
options: Middle of the first row of wrist bones
Little-finger side of the second row
Inside a tendon on the palm
questions.explanation: The lunate sits in the middle of the first row, between the scaphoid and the triquetrum.

synonyms: Cuneiform bone of the hand (older term)

content.origin: From the Latin word for three-cornered. It is shaped roughly like a small pyramid.
content.location: It sits in the first row of wrist bones on the little-finger side, next to the lunate. The pea-shaped pisiform rests on its palm side.
content.description: A pyramid-shaped bone with a small, smooth oval spot on its front where the pisiform sits.
content.function: It forms the little-finger side of the wrist and moves with its neighbours in the first row. It passes load through a cartilage pad to the ulna.
content.mnemonic: Tri means three, like a tricycle. Three corners, on the pinky side.
content.clinical: It is the second most often broken wrist bone. Usually a small chip breaks off its back surface.
content.hint: Look in the first row of wrist bones on the little-finger side, where a pea-shaped bone sits on top.

questions.text: Which bone sits on the palm side of the triquetrum?
questions.explanation: The little pea-shaped pisiform rests on the front, palm-side surface of the triquetrum.

content.origin: From the Latin words for pea and shape. It is small and round, just like a pea.
content.location: Find the crease on the palm side of your wrist. At its little-finger end you can feel this bone as a small, hard bump.
content.description: The smallest wrist bone. It sits inside the tendon of a forearm muscle called flexor carpi ulnaris.
content.function: It works like a tiny pulley inside the tendon, giving the muscle better leverage to bend the wrist. It also anchors a strong band across the wrist, the flexor retinaculum.
content.mnemonic: The pisiform is the pea you can feel at the pinky side of your wrist.
content.clinical: It forms one wall of a small tunnel called Guyon canal. The ulnar nerve and artery pass through it into the hand, so pressure here can numb the little finger.
content.hint: Feel for the tiny pea-shaped bump on the palm side, at the little-finger edge of the wrist.

questions.text: Why is the pisiform called a sesamoid bone?
options: It is the largest wrist bone
questions.explanation: A sesamoid bone grows inside a tendon. The pisiform grows inside the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, just as your kneecap sits inside a tendon.

content.origin: From the Greek for little table, an old word for a four-sided shape.
content.location: It sits in the second row of wrist bones on the thumb side, right at the base of the thumb's palm bone.
content.description: An odd-shaped bone with a saddle-shaped surface for the thumb and a groove for a wrist tendon.
content.function: It forms the saddle joint at the base of your thumb. This joint lets your thumb swing across your palm to touch each fingertip.
content.mnemonic: TrapeziUM sits under the thUMb. Both words end in UM.
content.clinical: The joint between this bone and the thumb is a very common place for arthritis. It can make opening jars or turning keys painful.
content.hint: Look in the second row of wrist bones, directly below the thumb's palm bone.

questions.text: What does the saddle joint between the trapezium and the thumb metacarpal let you do?
options: Touch your thumb to your fingertips
questions.explanation: The saddle-shaped trapezium lets the thumb swing across the palm to touch the other fingers. This move is called opposition.

questions.text: How can you tell the trapezium from the trapezoid?
options: The trapezium is under the thumb
The trapezium is under the little finger
The trapezium is in the first row
The trapezium is inside a tendon
questions.explanation: Remember trapeziUM under the thUMb. The trapezoid sits right next to it, under the index finger.

content.origin: From the Greek for table-shaped. It is the smaller neighbour of the trapezium.
content.location: It sits in the second row of wrist bones, between the trapezium and the capitate, at the base of the index finger's palm bone.
content.description: A small wedge-shaped bone, the smallest in the second row.
content.function: It holds the base of the index finger's palm bone firmly in place. This makes your index finger a steady pillar for pointing and pinching.
content.mnemonic: TrapezOID is the Other one. It sits beside the trapezium, under the index finger.
content.clinical: It is rarely broken on its own, because it is well protected and tightly tied to its neighbours.
content.hint: Look in the second row of wrist bones, between the thumb-side bone and the big central bone.

questions.text: Which metacarpal does the trapezoid mainly support?
questions.explanation: The trapezoid sits at the base of the second metacarpal, the palm bone of your index finger.

content.origin: From the Latin word for head. Its rounded head fits snugly into the first row of wrist bones.
content.location: It sits in the centre of the second row of wrist bones, at the base of the middle finger's palm bone.
content.description: The biggest wrist bone. Its round head nestles into a hollow made by the scaphoid and lunate, like a ball in a cup.
content.function: It is the keystone of the wrist, the centre that wrist movement turns around. It carries force from your middle finger to the lunate and radius.
content.mnemonic: Capitate is the Captain: the biggest bone, standing in the centre.
content.clinical: It is the first wrist bone to turn from cartilage into bone in a baby. That makes it useful for judging a child's bone age on an X-ray.
content.hint: Look for the biggest wrist bone, in the middle of the second row, below the middle finger.

questions.text: Which is the largest wrist bone?
questions.explanation: The capitate is the largest wrist bone. It sits in the centre of the second row.

content.origin: From the Latin word for hook. It has a small hook that sticks out towards the palm.
content.location: It sits in the second row of wrist bones on the little-finger side, at the base of the ring and little finger palm bones.
content.description: A wedge-shaped bone with a hook, the hook of hamate, that juts out towards your palm.
content.function: It supports the palm bones of your ring and little fingers. Its hook anchors the band that forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.
content.mnemonic: Hamate has a hook. Hang your ring finger and pinky on it.
content.clinical: A golf club, racquet or bat handle pressing into the palm can snap the hook. It also borders Guyon canal, where the ulnar nerve passes into the hand.
content.hint: Look in the second row of wrist bones on the little-finger side, and find the hook.

questions.text: What feature gives the hamate its name?
questions.explanation: Hamate comes from the Latin word for hook, after the small hook that sticks out towards the palm.

questions.text: In which sport is a broken hook of hamate typically seen?
questions.explanation: When a golf club, racquet or bat handle presses hard into the palm, it can snap the hook of hamate.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the wrist. These are the bones of your palm, just past the wrist.
content.location: It sits in the palm in line with your thumb. Palm bones are numbered one to five, starting at the thumb.
content.description: The shortest and thickest palm bone. It sits at an angle to the others, which lets the thumb face your fingers.
content.function: It lets your thumb move on its own and with real power. You use it every time you grip a bottle or pinch a coin.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: the thumb is number one. Make a fist, and its head is your thumb knuckle.
content.clinical: A Bennett fracture is a break at the base of this bone that runs into the thumb joint. It often happens when a clenched fist hits something hard.
content.hint: Look in the palm, in line with the thumb.

questions.text: Which metacarpal is the shortest and thickest?
questions.explanation: The first metacarpal, behind the thumb, is the shortest and thickest palm bone.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the wrist. Meta means beyond, and karpos means wrist.
content.location: It sits in the palm in line with your index finger. Counting from the thumb, it is number two.
content.description: Usually the longest palm bone. Its notched base locks against the trapezoid like a puzzle piece.
content.function: It forms a firm, fixed pillar for your index finger. That steadiness helps with fine work like writing or threading a needle.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: the index finger is number two. Its head is your pointer knuckle.
content.clinical: Because its base is locked in so firmly, a hard knock on this bone travels straight into the wrist bones.
content.hint: Look in the palm, in line with the pointing finger.

questions.text: Which wrist bone does the second metacarpal meet?
questions.explanation: The base of the second metacarpal locks into the trapezoid.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the wrist. It is the central bone of your palm.
content.location: It sits in the middle of the palm, in line with your middle finger. Counting from the thumb, it is number three.
content.description: A long palm bone with a small bony point on the back of its base, called the styloid process.
content.function: It is the central and steadiest pillar of your hand, lined up with the capitate in the wrist.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: the middle finger is number three. Its head is the knuckle in the middle of your fist.
content.clinical: The small point at its base can form an extra bony lump on the back of the hand, called a carpal boss.
content.hint: Look in the centre of the palm, in line with the middle finger.

questions.text: Which wrist bone does the third metacarpal meet?
questions.explanation: The third metacarpal sits on the capitate, the big central wrist bone.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the wrist. It is the ring finger's bone in the palm.
content.location: It sits in the palm in line with your ring finger. Counting from the thumb, it is number four.
content.description: A slim palm bone, thinner than the second and third. Its base can move a little more than theirs.
content.function: It supports your ring finger. Its small bit of movement helps your palm cup around a ball or a glass.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: the ring finger is number four. Its head is the knuckle just behind your ring.
content.clinical: A punch can break the neck of this bone, often together with the fifth metacarpal next to it.
content.hint: Look in the palm, in line with the ring finger.

questions.text: Which wrist bone does the fourth metacarpal mainly meet?
questions.explanation: The fourth metacarpal rests mainly on the hamate, and it also touches the capitate.

content.origin: From the Greek for beyond the wrist. It is the little finger's bone in the palm.
content.location: It sits in the palm along the little-finger edge of your hand. Counting from the thumb, it is number five.
content.description: A slim palm bone. Its base, where it meets the hamate, moves more than that of any other metacarpal.
content.function: It supports your little finger and lets the outer edge of your palm curl around objects for a firm grip.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: the little finger is number five, last in line. Its head is your pinky knuckle.
content.clinical: A boxer fracture is a break in the neck of this bone. It often happens when someone punches a wall or another hard surface.
content.hint: Look in the palm, along the little-finger edge of the hand.

questions.text: A boxer fracture most often breaks which bone?
questions.explanation: A boxer fracture is a break in the neck of the fifth metacarpal, the palm bone of the little finger.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Your finger bones stand in rows, like soldiers in line.
content.location: It is the first bone of your thumb, just past the thumb knuckle.
content.description: The longer of the thumb's two bones. Its cupped base fits over the round head of the metacarpal like a socket.
content.function: It forms the thumb knuckle joint with the metacarpal, helping your thumb bend and straighten as you grip.
content.mnemonic: Proximal means closest. It is the thumb bone closest to your palm.
content.clinical: If a break here heals with a twist, the thumb can end up pointing the wrong way. That is why these breaks must be lined up carefully.
content.hint: Find the thumb bone closest to the palm.

questions.text: How many phalanges, or finger bones, does the thumb have?
questions.explanation: The thumb has just two, a proximal and a distal phalanx. The other fingers have three each.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Each finger has its bones lined up in a row.
content.location: It is the first bone of your index finger, just past the knuckle.
content.description: The longest of the index finger's three bones. Its cupped base fits over the round knuckle like a cup on a ball.
content.function: It forms the knuckle joint, which lets your pointing finger bend, straighten and spread away from the others.
content.mnemonic: Proximal sounds like proximity, which means closeness. It is the finger bone closest to your palm.
content.clinical: A break here can leave the finger twisted if it heals out of line. Then the finger may cross over its neighbour when you make a fist.
content.hint: Find the pointing finger bone closest to the palm.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Your middle finger has three of these bones in a row.
content.location: It is the first bone of your middle finger, just past the knuckle.
content.description: The longest bone of your longest finger. Its hollow base sits over the round knuckle.
content.function: It forms the knuckle joint of your middle finger, letting it bend, straighten and move sideways.
content.mnemonic: Proximal is closest to your palm. Think P for proximal and P for palm.
content.clinical: Finger breaks near the knuckle need careful lining up. If they heal with a twist, the fingers overlap when you grip.
content.hint: Find the bone of the longest finger nearest the palm.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Like soldiers, the ring finger's bones march in a row.
content.location: It is the first bone of your ring finger, just past the knuckle, right where a ring sits.
content.description: The longest of the ring finger's three bones, with a cupped base that fits the round knuckle.
content.function: It forms the knuckle joint of your ring finger, letting it bend, straighten and spread.
content.mnemonic: Proximal means closest to the palm. Your ring slides onto this bone.
content.clinical: If this bone heals with a twist after a break, the ring finger can drift across its neighbour when you curl your hand.
content.hint: Find the ring finger bone closest to the palm.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Even your little finger has three in its row.
content.location: It is the first bone of your little finger, just past the knuckle.
content.description: The longest of the little finger's three bones, though still small. Its cupped base fits the knuckle.
content.function: It forms the knuckle joint that lets your little finger bend, straighten and spread wide.
content.mnemonic: Proximal means closest to the palm. Little finger, first bone, right next to the knuckle.
content.clinical: A break here that heals with a twist can make the little finger overlap the ring finger when you make a fist.
content.hint: Find the little finger bone closest to the palm.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This one stands in the middle of the line.
content.location: It is the middle bone of your index finger. The thumb has no bone like this.
content.description: A short bone, shorter than the one below it, with a joint at each end.
content.function: It gives your finger a second bending joint. A forearm tendon, flexor digitorum superficialis, pulls on it to bend that joint.
content.mnemonic: Middle means in the middle, and the thumb skips it.
content.clinical: Damage to the tendons around the middle finger joint can bend the finger into odd shapes, called boutonniere or swan-neck deformity.
content.hint: Find the middle bone of the pointing finger.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the middle soldier of three.
content.location: It is the middle bone of your middle finger. The thumb has no middle bone at all.
content.description: A short bone with a joint at both ends, like a link in a chain.
content.function: It adds a second hinge so your finger can curl around things. A long forearm tendon, flexor digitorum superficialis, pulls on it to bend that hinge.
content.mnemonic: The middle bone of the middle finger. Easy: middle, middle, and the thumb skips it.
content.clinical: Jamming a finger can hurt the joint at this bone's base. If the tendons there are damaged, the finger may set in a boutonniere or swan-neck shape.
content.hint: Find the middle bone of the longest finger.

questions.text: Which digit has no middle phalanx?
questions.explanation: The thumb has only two bones, a proximal and a distal phalanx. Every other finger has a middle one too.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. Three stand in the ring finger's row, and this is the middle one.
content.location: It is the middle bone of your ring finger, between the first bone and the tip.
content.description: A short bone with a joint at both ends, shorter than the first bone of the finger.
content.function: It gives the ring finger its second bending joint, so the finger can wrap around a handle. A forearm tendon pulls on it to bend.
content.mnemonic: Middle bone, middle position. Only the thumb goes without one.
content.clinical: A ball hitting the fingertip can jam the joint at this bone's base. Tendon damage there can lead to a boutonniere or swan-neck shape.
content.hint: Find the middle bone of the ring finger.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the little finger's middle soldier.
content.location: It is the middle bone of your little finger. The thumb is the only digit without one.
content.description: A small, short bone with a joint at each end, the tiniest middle bone in the hand.
content.function: It adds a second bend to your little finger, helping it hook around objects. A forearm tendon pulls on it to bend.
content.mnemonic: Middle means middle. Four fingers have one, and the thumb skips it.
content.clinical: Injured tendons around the joint at this bone can leave the finger stuck in a boutonniere or swan-neck shape.
content.hint: Find the middle bone of the little finger.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the soldier at the very front.
content.location: It is the tip bone of your thumb, under the thumbnail.
content.description: A small bone that spreads into a rough, flat tip. That tip holds up the soft pad and the nail.
content.function: It supports your thumb tip for touch and pinch. A deep tendon from the forearm pulls on it to bend the tip.
content.mnemonic: Distal sounds like distant. It is the bone farthest from your palm.
content.clinical: Crushing the thumb tip, for example in a door, often breaks its tip, called a tuft fracture. A tendon tear at its base stops the tip from straightening.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the thumb.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the last soldier, at the front of the line.
content.location: It is the tip bone of your index finger, under the nail.
content.description: A tiny bone with a rough, flattened tip that holds up your fingertip pad and nail.
content.function: It supports your fingertip for fine touch and pinching. A deep tendon pulls on it to bend the tip.
content.mnemonic: Distal means distant from the palm. It is the fingertip bone.
content.clinical: If a ball strikes the fingertip, the tendon that straightens it can tear away at this bone. The tip then droops, which is called mallet finger.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the pointing finger.

questions.text: What is mallet finger?
options: A tendon injury at the tip bone, so the fingertip droops
A break of the fifth metacarpal
questions.explanation: In mallet finger, the tendon that straightens the fingertip tears where it joins the distal phalanx. The tip droops and cannot straighten.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the front of the line on your middle finger.
content.location: It is the tip bone of your middle finger, under the nail.
content.description: A small bone that widens into a rough, flat tip, like a tiny spade supporting the pad and nail.
content.function: It gives your fingertip a firm base for feeling textures and gripping. A deep tendon pulls on it to curl the tip.
content.mnemonic: Distal is distant: the bone farthest from your palm, right at the tip.
content.clinical: Fingertips shut in a car door often break this bone's tip, a tuft fracture. A torn tendon at its base causes mallet finger.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the longest finger.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the ring finger's front-line soldier.
content.location: It is the tip bone of your ring finger, under the nail.
content.description: A tiny bone with a rough, flattened end that props up the fingertip pad and nail.
content.function: It supports the ring fingertip so you can feel and grip. A deep forearm tendon pulls on it to bend the tip.
content.mnemonic: Distal means distant from the palm, so it is the fingertip.
content.clinical: Crushing the tip can break this bone, a tuft fracture. A tear of the tendon that straightens it at its base makes the tip droop, called mallet finger.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the ring finger.

content.origin: From the Greek word phalanx, a line of soldiers. This is the smallest soldier at the front of the line.
content.location: It is the tip bone of your little finger, under the smallest nail.
content.description: A very small bone with a rough, flat tip that supports the fingertip pad and nail.
content.function: It supports the little fingertip. A deep tendon pulls on it to bend the tip when you grip.
content.mnemonic: Distal is distant, at the tip of the finger. Little finger, last bone.
content.clinical: Crushing the fingertip can break its tip, a tuft fracture. A tendon tear at its base lets the tip droop, called mallet finger.
content.hint: Find the tip bone of the little finger.
